title: Modernising elections: finance, registration, votes at 16 and online threats
label: 20 October 2026 · Modernising Elections evidence session
summary: Ministers set out how the Representation of the People Bill, the government response to the Rycroft review and other measures aim to reduce foreign and illicit money in UK politics, expand voter registration and enfranchise 16–17-year-olds, while recognising gaps on the unregulated period, pilots for automated registration and online disinformation. They committed to further work with the Electoral Commission, local authorities, DCMS and other bodies and to write back on several detailed points.

glossary.definition: The government's bill proposing changes to how UK elections are run, including registration, ID and finance rules.
The UK's independent elections regulator that sets guidance and enforces rules on voting and political finance.
The 365 days before an election when special spending and reporting rules apply.
A temporary ban on political donations made in cryptocurrency until they can be properly traced and regulated.
A system that adds eligible people to the electoral register using government-held data instead of requiring them to apply.
A digital or paper certificate electors could use as ID at polling stations.
2023 UK law giving Ofcom powers to require platforms to tackle online harms, including some disinformation.
A cross-government group (MHCLG, DCMS, Home Office, etc.) coordinating work to protect elections.

glossary.term: Joint Election Security and Preparedness Unit
glossary.definition: A unit that brings together government, security agencies and the Electoral Commission during election periods.
EU law that places duties on platforms to manage risks from their services, including political disinformation.
The proposal to lower the voting age so 16–17-year-olds can vote in UK parliamentary elections.

chapters.title: Political finance and foreign interference
chapters.takeaway: Ministers accept Rycroft's recommendations and aim to tighten donor checks, limit risky routes like crypto, and work with the Electoral Commission to strengthen transparency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How confident are you that your reforms will stop foreign interference as set out in Philip Rycroft's review?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We accepted Rycroft's recommendations: make donations traceable, strengthen 'know-your-donor' checks, work with the Electoral Commission on tougher rules and fines, and introduce a moratorium on crypto donations until tracing is possible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If parties must do risk assessments of donors, will the Government provide guidance so assessments are consistent?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Yes. We'll work with all parties, the Electoral Commission and the Speaker’s Committee to make rules clear and ensure parties know how to comply before major elections.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why doesn't the Bill show the mechanism for lifting the crypto moratorium?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: The moratorium is in place now. Lifting it would need primary legislation after Parliament considers the Electoral Commission's work on how to trace crypto; we want to avoid the current risks.

turns.speaker: Mr Gagan Mohindra
turns.text: On company donations: you use a profit test over five years—won't successful companies still donate multiple times using the same profit?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We chose a five-year post-tax profit window to show long-term UK economic activity and close shell-company loopholes, while allowing genuine local firms to donate.

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: We recognise the concern and will bring forward proposals in the Lords to tackle ways a company might multiply donations unfairly.

chapters.title: The regulated period and unregulated campaigning
chapters.takeaway: Ministers see value in the regulated period but accept Rycroft's point: more work is needed to prevent activity shifting into unregulated times.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Does the distinction between regulated and unregulated periods still make sense when campaigning is effectively continuous?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: The regulated period gives clarity on spending and transparency, but we must guard against activity outside it. We don't want to overburden volunteers; the Electoral Commission must clarify rules for off-period activity.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Has the Government asked the Electoral Commission to start work on this?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: We've begun conversations and are working with the Commission on many issues including the regulated period, but they don't yet have a dedicated workstream on this; we'll progress it quickly and update the Committee.

turns.speaker: Mr Lee Dillon
turns.text: Can you share timetables for the guidance the Electoral Commission is preparing?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: I don't have the timetable now but will share it with the Committee once available.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have you compared international approaches on foreign interference?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: Yes—regular dialogue with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and European partners; we learn from different models but adapt to our circumstances.

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: The Defending Democracy Taskforce, across several departments, coordinates our whole-of-government response to these threats.

chapters.title: Overseas donations and task groups
chapters.takeaway: A task-and-finish group will test caps and residency tests for donors, but blanket caps raise tracing problems and details and timing are still being developed.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: Will the task-and-finish team consider universal donations caps to handle overseas donations?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Terms of reference are being finalised. The team will examine residency tests, the Rycroft-recommended £100,000 cap, and other measures; blanket caps are tricky because they make tracing harder.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: When will that task group start?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: It's a priority and we are pressing colleagues; we'll share timescales with the Committee as soon as we can.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: Some witnesses suggested a £1 million cap—are you concerned about that?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: That seems high; Rycroft's lower £100,000 recommendation is the balance we think is right for now, though debate continues.

chapters.title: Registration, automated registration pilots and votes at 16
chapters.takeaway: The Government aims to extend registration and enfranchise 16–17-year-olds before the next general election, but pilots, data-sharing, local capacity and fairness of partial roll-outs remain unresolved.

turns.speaker: Lewis Cocking
turns.text: Will automated voter registration (AVR) cover the whole country before the next general election?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: That's our ambition. We're testing automated systems in pilots and working with local authorities and the Electoral Commission to build evidence; we want AVR in place before the next scheduled general election if possible.

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: AVR is complex—Australia's system took years. We'll pilot in diverse areas and set criteria with the Electoral Commission to avoid unfair local differences; we'll work with political parties too.

turns.speaker: Lewis Cocking
turns.text: If only some local areas pilot AVR, could a single constituency have voters treated differently?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: We understand that risk. We will design pilots carefully and consult the Committee and parties; I can't answer hypotheticals about a future election result.

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We will aim for a fair geographic spread in pilots. Practical steps already taken include adding an opt-in for the electoral register to some DVLA processes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Wales has already piloted AVR—how are you working with them?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: Wales registers residents for Senedd elections and doesn't require nationality checks—UK parliamentary registration needs nationality data, which makes English pilots more complex.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Local authorities will need data cleansers and extra capacity to join data—how will you resource that?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Electoral teams need support. I'll press the Treasury via the Local Government Association and Ministers to ensure electoral teams are funded, because these staff run frequent elections nationally.

turns.speaker: Mr Will Forster
turns.text: Votes at 16 is in your manifesto—if there were an early election, would 16–17-year-olds be excluded?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: If an early poll came before we complete the roll-out and preparatory work it might not be feasible. Our plan is to have votes at 16 in place by the next scheduled general election, supported by engagement funding and curriculum work.

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: We're working with DfE on citizenship education and with the Electoral Commission on impartial communications to prepare young people for voting.

turns.speaker: Mr Will Forster
turns.text: Will the Democratic Engagement Fund reach the young people who are hardest to reach?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Yes—the fund targets groups aged 5–25, including disadvantaged, homeless, disabled and frequently moving young people. We will evaluate the pilots closely.

chapters.title: Voter ID, online misinformation and electoral law
chapters.takeaway: The Government widened acceptable ID to include UK bank cards to reduce people being turned away, but concerns remain about unbanked voters, digital certificates, social media duties and the complexity of election law.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: Why are you adding bank cards as ID rather than digital voter certificates?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We aren't prioritising bank cards over digital IDs; bank cards are widely held, can be checked at polling stations and were requested by groups worried about people being turned away. Digital certificates exist but demand has been low and are under review.

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: The voter authority certificate remains available but has had little take-up. We paused further roll-out while we reviewed practicalities and workload at polling stations.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: Is there a risk bank-card ID will exclude unbanked or disadvantaged voters?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We recognise that risk, but evidence shows the majority of eligible voters have a UK bank card. Widening acceptable ID aims to reduce, not increase, the number turned away.

turns.speaker: Mr Lee Dillon
turns.text: Why not scrap ID requirements altogether, given documented cases of impersonation have been very rare?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: That is a policy choice. The current approach keeps photographic ID while widening options to avoid disenfranchisement; we are focussing on workable measures for polling staff and voters.

turns.speaker: Mr Lee Dillon
turns.text: On online disinformation: why didn't the Online Safety Act prioritise election offences, and will you adopt measures like the EU's Digital Services Act to force platforms to act?

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: DCMS leads on the Online Safety Act. We will feed your questions back; we already use the Joint Election Security and Preparedness Unit to coordinate government action during campaigns and to work with platforms in real time.

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: We are pressing platforms for greater transparency and cooperation. The Prime Minister has prioritised information defence and created a National Centre for Information Defence; we'll write to the Committee about how it will operate.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Electoral law is fragmented—will you commit to consolidation, perhaps via the Law Commission?

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Consolidation is sensible but huge. It would take time and cross-party support—possibly more than one Parliament. For now our priority is delivering the Representation of the People Bill and the Rycroft changes.

turns.speaker: Stuart Ison
turns.text: We recognise concerns about complexity and will keep the issue under review; guidance aims to help practitioners in the meantime.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You agreed to write back on AVR pilots, the Welsh experience, unregulated-period work by the Electoral Commission, the Online Safety Act overlaps, the new information-defence centre and timelines for donations work.

turns.speaker: Florence Eshalomi
turns.text: Yes—we will provide the Committee with further details and updates on those points.
